abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for analyzing the complexity of continuous problems that fundamentally reconceptualizes the relationship between problem structure and computational cost. Traditional complexity analysis relies on fixed information classes and asymptotic classifications, yet this approach often fails to capture the nuanced interplay between algorithm design and problem characteristics. Our framework replaces static complexity models with a dynamic analysis that tracks how computational difficulty evolves with algorithmic choices. By introducing the concept of complexity-adaptive information operators, we demonstrate that problems previously classified as intractable under classical settings admit polynomial-time algorithms when information acquisition is treated as an adaptive process rather than a predetermined sequence. This perspective shift reveals that tractability depends not merely on problem parameters but on the algorithm's capacity to sense and exploit problem structure dynamically. The framework establishes deep connections between information-based complexity and modern optimal transport theory, yielding a unified treatment of discretization and information complexity that opens new research directions. We provide matching upper and lower bounds demonstrating that our characterization captures the true computational complexity in this expanded model. This paradigm innovation challenges established classifications in continuous complexity theory and provides new tools for analyzing high-dimensional problems in approximation and integration.

We establish significantly sharper complexity bounds for numerical integration over high-dimensional weighted Sobolev spaces, addressing a central open problem in the theory of tractability. Previous analyses yielded complexity bounds that are tight only up to logarithmic factors, leaving substantial gaps between necessary and sufficient conditions across different weight regimes. Through a refined decomposition technique that exploits the tensor product structure of weighted spaces with product weights, we derive lower bounds that match existing upper bounds up to constants. Our analysis reveals that the tractability exponent can be characterized precisely as a function of the weight parameters, significantly sharpening all previously known results. The key innovation lies in a novel method for constructing hard instances that simultaneously stress multiple aspects of the integration problem, requiring algorithms to balance contributions across all dimensions. For the upper bound, we construct carefully designed quasi-Monte Carlo rules with optimal convergence rates, providing an efficient algorithm whose complexity matches the lower bound exactly. These results resolve longstanding open problems regarding the complexity of weighted integration and provide a complete characterization of the tractability landscape. The techniques developed here extend to other high-dimensional problems in approximation and integration, offering a template for refined complexity analysis in information-based complexity.

We present a new computational paradigm for high-dimensional approximation that fundamentally shifts how complexity reduction is achieved in practice. Existing algorithms for high-dimensional problems typically rely on fixed basis representations or predetermined sampling strategies, approaches that fundamentally limit adaptability to problem-specific structure. Our system integrates real-time complexity monitoring directly into the algorithmic process, maintaining continuous estimates of local approximation error to dynamically allocate computational resources across different problem regions. This represents a paradigm shift from offline complexity analysis to online complexity management, where algorithmic decisions are guided by emerging information about problem structure. The framework unifies insights from information-based complexity with modern machine learning techniques, creating an architecture that achieves near-optimal convergence rates without requiring a priori knowledge of smoothness parameters. We prove complexity guarantees for the system showing that the approach achieves the same order of convergence as theoretically optimal algorithms while adapting automatically to problem difficulty. Numerical experiments on problems in uncertainty quantification and parametric PDEs demonstrate that this tight integration of complexity theory and algorithm design enables tractable computation for problems where traditional approaches fail. This work establishes that paradigm shifts in computational strategy can unlock computational feasibility for previously intractable high-dimensional continuous problems.

We develop an algorithm for high-dimensional integration that substantially improves convergence rates compared to existing quasi-Monte Carlo and lattice methods. The approach combines an adaptive sampling strategy with an optimized weight structure that better exploits function smoothness than current techniques. Unlike previous adaptive methods whose overhead often negates theoretical advantages, our algorithm achieves convergence rates that adapt to problem difficulty while maintaining practical efficiency. Complexity analysis establishes upper bounds that improve upon existing results by a factor of n^(−1/2) in the high-dimensional regime, where n denotes the number of function evaluations, with matching lower bounds demonstrating optimality. The key innovation lies in a two-stage estimation procedure that first identifies regions of significant contribution and then applies concentrated sampling in these regions while maintaining global coverage. Implementation considerations are addressed, including strategies for practical weight selection and sample allocation that preserve theoretical guarantees. Numerical experiments on standard test problems in uncertainty quantification demonstrate significant practical gains over established methods at comparable computational cost. The principles underlying this algorithm extend to broader classes of high-dimensional approximation and optimization problems, providing improved tools for applications in computational finance and engineering design.
